title: Monitor Object Pattern
oneLiner: Ensures only one thread executes any of an object's methods at a time, with built-in waiting for the right conditions.

hero.name: The Sentinel
hero.catchphrase: One thread in this room at a time. Everyone else waits their turn, safely.
hero.power: Synchronizes every method on an object so only one thread executes any of them at once, coordinating waiting threads through built-in conditions.
hero.weakness: A lock around too much code turns parallel work into serial work — an overly broad monitor kills the very concurrency you needed in the first place.
hero.origin: The Sentinel appeared after a shared BankAccount object let two threads both read a balance of $100, both approve a $60 withdrawal, and both succeed — leaving the account at -$20 with nobody noticing the race.

story.problem: Two threads both call `withdraw(60)` on a shared BankAccount with a $100 balance at nearly the same instant. Both read $100, both see enough funds, both succeed — draining the account to -$20.
story.solution: The Sentinel wraps every method on BankAccount so only one thread can execute any of them at a time. The second `withdraw()` call simply waits until the first one fully finishes.
story.result: Only one withdrawal executes at a time. The second thread sees the correctly updated balance and is safely rejected if funds are now insufficient.

before: Multiple threads can execute methods on the same object simultaneously
Reads and writes can interleave unpredictably
Race conditions silently corrupt shared state
after: Only one thread executes any method on the object at a time
Shared state stays consistent no matter how many threads call in

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A bank account log shows two withdrawals of $60 both succeeding against a $100 balance.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: The account is at negative twenty dollars. Both withdrawals read the same starting balance and both went through!

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Sentinel stands at the account's only door, letting exactly one thread in at a time.
panels.speaker: The Sentinel
panels.dialogue: Stop letting threads barge in simultaneously. One thread executes a method on this account at a time. Everyone else waits.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: withdraw() acquires the object's lock before running, releases it after. A second call simply waits its turn.
panels.speaker: The Sentinel
panels.dialogue: The second withdraw() call doesn't even start until the first is completely done. It sees the TRUE, updated balance.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The second $60 withdrawal now correctly fails against the true $40 remaining balance.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: The second withdrawal now correctly sees $40 left and gets rejected. No more phantom negative balances.

useWhen: Multiple threads share access to the same mutable object, and unsynchronized access could corrupt its state.
You need a thread to wait for a specific condition on the shared object (like 'balance is sufficient') before proceeding.
The correctness cost of a race condition (financial data, inventory counts) is high enough to justify the synchronization overhead.
avoidWhen: The object's state is immutable, or only ever accessed from a single thread — there's no race to prevent.
The lock would need to cover a large, slow operation, serializing work that should run in parallel.
A lock-free or higher-level concurrency primitive (atomic operations, channels) fits the problem better.
commonMistakes: Locking around more code than necessary, turning genuinely parallelizable work into a serial bottleneck.
Forgetting that a monitor only protects against concurrent access WITHIN itself — external state accessed outside the monitor is still unprotected.
Creating deadlocks by acquiring multiple monitors' locks in inconsistent orders across different code paths.
Using a monitor as a substitute for actually thinking about the concurrency model, instead of designing for it deliberately.
explanation.realWorldExample: Java's `synchronized` methods, C#'s `lock` statement, and any class using a mutex to guard all of its public methods are Monitor Object in practice — it's one of the most fundamental concurrency patterns in mainstream languages.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Isn't this just... putting a lock around a class?

conversation.speaker: The Sentinel
conversation.message: That's the mechanism, yes — but the discipline matters. EVERY method that touches shared state needs the same lock, consistently, or you get partial protection that's worse than none at all — false confidence.

conversation.speaker: The Sentinel
conversation.message: Locking too broadly. Wrap an entire slow operation in my protection and you've turned parallel work into a single-file line — sometimes worse for performance than having no synchronization design at all.

codeBattle.scenario: Your inventory service lets two warehouse workers simultaneously decrement the same product's stock count, and under load the count occasionally goes negative because both reads happen before either write.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Sentinel ensures only one thread can execute the stock-decrement method at a time, eliminating the read-then-write race that let the count go negative.

quiz.question: What guarantee does a Monitor Object provide?
options: Only one thread can execute any of the object's synchronized methods at a time
Every thread executes methods simultaneously without any waiting
The object can never be accessed by more than one thread ever
Method calls are automatically retried on failure
quiz.answer: Only one thread can execute any of the object's synchronized methods at a time
quiz.explanation: This mutual exclusion across all synchronized methods is the defining guarantee of Monitor Object.

quiz.question: What's the classic bug Monitor Object prevents?
options: A race condition where two threads read stale shared state before either writes an update
A memory leak from unclosed file handles
An interface mismatch between two classes
A missing null check on user input
quiz.answer: A race condition where two threads read stale shared state before either writes an update
quiz.explanation: The classic 'check-then-act' race (like the bank withdrawal example) is exactly what mutual exclusion prevents.

quiz.question: What's a common mistake that reduces Monitor Object's effectiveness?
options: Locking around only some methods that touch shared state, leaving others unsynchronized
Synchronizing every method that touches shared state consistently
Using a mutex to guard the object's methods
Applying it to genuinely shared mutable state
quiz.answer: Locking around only some methods that touch shared state, leaving others unsynchronized
quiz.explanation: Partial synchronization gives false confidence — any unsynchronized method leaves a gap for the same race condition.

quiz.question: What's a mainstream language feature that implements Monitor Object directly?
quiz.explanation: `synchronized` methods are a built-in, language-level implementation of the Monitor Object pattern.
